body: Dispatches, reports, audits, and `see` lists cite ids; a rename breaks every one of them silently.

Permanence includes reachability through every reader - get, see-citations, batch membership - across an archive sweep; a mover that strands any one reader breaks the rule even though the id still exists on disk (batch 22 T1: three reader paths closed one by one).

A non-standing entry in an area with empty globs other than global (`process` in the seed) never loads with a file. A global entry loads with every file through `houserules for` and joins every audit package (a task audit leaves out an entry tagged `controller` unless `--ids` names it), but renders into no rules file (batch 11).
After filing, run `houserules for <a file the rule governs>` and confirm the entry appears.

The kit's non-standing procedure rules in the glob-less `process` area load by citation instead: a kit-owned skill or agent template names the id, and its reader runs `houserules get <id>`. `check-knowledge` fails a cited id that the base does not hold. Such an entry never joins an audit package by area; name it in `--ids` to audit against it. `process.risk-tiers`, `process.severity-by-impact`, `process.bounded-review-loop`, `process.knowledge-earns-its-place`, and `process.parallel-on-disjoint-files` load this way.

A non-standing `process` entry also loads through two paths. The controller reads its summary at the session ritual's `houserules index --area process`. An agent receives its id on the `Knowledge:` line of a dispatch.

Make a process rule standing only when every session must carry it. Give the `controller` tag to a rule that only the controller can break: a task audit leaves the entry out of its package unless `--ids` names it (`knowledge-base.controller-rules-are-tagged`).

A `check` needs an audit loading path too: it joins the package when its entry is `standing`, sits in a touched or global area (any kind, not only rule and invariant), or is named in `--ids`. A task audit leaves out the check of an entry tagged `controller` unless `--ids` names that entry.

source.ref: batch 5 branch review, issue 1

body: Invented claims read plausibly; that is what makes them dangerous.
When two sources disagree, read the code and record which one the entry follows.
A shipped template or seed names no root-only id, path, or command; verify every reference resolves in a fresh install before syncing the root copy (batch 7 task 3).

Run every command block you ship exactly as printed, top to bottom, in the environment the reader will have (a fresh directory for a quick start). A block that needs unstated context, or that resolves differently than printed (an unpinned git spec), fails this rule (batch 13: a quick start that exited 1 as printed, an install form floating to the default branch, a kit-only mechanism shipped as generic).

The walk includes a control: when a line looks optional, re-run the block without it and confirm the block then fails — that proves the line load-bearing instead of decorative (batch 18 T6 r2: the quick start's `houserules update --dir .` line was proven load-bearing by exactly this control). Sweeps keyed on deleted-tool names miss claims keyed on surviving names (batch 18 branch review: a design-doc aside naming `bin/houserules.mjs` escaped a sweep that grepped for the deleted wrappers); sweep for the claim's subject too.

A corrected measurement sweeps its dependents: when a sentence is corrected, re-open every sentence that cites, paraphrases, or leans on it — not only the lines the round edited; antecedents drift when their referent is repaired (batch 19 T2 r2, README:110).

An amendment re-derives the entry's summary from the amended body before filing - the summary is the half that renders into the loaded rules files, so a stale summary ships wider than the body it contradicts (batch 20 T3: two amended entries kept summaries their own new bodies had overturned; batch 20 T4: two shipped doc comments stated non-facts their own commits made false).

Before shipping a uniqueness or attribution sentence ('the only', 'caused by'), run the enumeration that would falsify it against the tree at HEAD - batch 21's two instances (a misattributed gate failure; a false only-bin-that-walks claim) were each falsifiable by one grep the writer did not run.

A rewritten doc comment is teaching prose under this rule: re-derive caller counts, uniqueness claims, and cross-references from the tree at the revision under edit, never from the pre-rewrite text or another agent's summary (batch 22 T3a/T3c).

Prose stating an invariant about commit history ('always', 'never', 'by the time it reaches main') enumerates every author class that writes such commits - bot-authored release and dependency commits included; a release-please extra-files commit falsified one such 'always' in batch 24.

When a commit closes an item, grep the tracked docs for that item's id in the same commit: the closing commit owns every sentence that scheduled the work (batch 24 close, three occurrences of the same forward-reading class).

A premise in a spec or a brief about what another module does is a claim: open that module's doc or code before a doc comment or a dispatch restates it (batch 28 task 6: 'update overwrites kit-owned files' went from the spec into the brief, a module doc, and the README, while `update` keeps a locally modified file).
One quoted message for two runs is two claims: copy the text from the log of each run (batch 28: the CodeQL message of PR 34 has its two versions in the other order than the quote taken from PR 33).

fields.summary: Ask the user when information is missing. Do not assume.
Start each batch with a brainstorming session or a written spec; get the user's approval before implementing.
body: Use the superpowers brainstorming and spec skills when the plugin is installed; otherwise write the spec by hand. Specs live in `docs/specs/`.
The order is strict: spec, then plan. A plan written before its approved spec is nil - deleted and the planning phase redone from the spec, never re-anchored (owner ruling, batch 18, 2026-09-05).
A light-tier change (`process.risk-tiers`) has no plan. The body of its backlog item is the written spec, and the owner approves it before implementation.
The controller writes briefs from the spec and plan; a silent omission surfaces only in review, one round late (batch 3, task 3).
When a brief and the spec disagree, the spec wins and the disagreement is a ruling to record.

source.ref: batch 3 branch review, uncovered_findings; task 3 review, finding 2

body: The recurring failure is not fabrication but drift: the work is right while the sentence describing it cites a capture that is not there, quotes a line the capture lost, or keeps a rationale a later verification overturned (batch 16 tasks 2 and 5).

The check is mechanical: for each named file, open it; for each quoted line, grep it; for each number, recompute it from the artifact. A reviewer does exactly this, so a report that skips it converts Minor findings into review rounds.
A reversed trend is worth recording too: name the pattern in the review when it appears, and name its reversal when a later round demonstrates it (batch 16 task 2 round 2).

A SHIPPED doc or comment sentence stating a measurement is a claim like a report sentence (ruled batch 18): it cites a retained capture at a durable path, and a fix round's sweep re-opens every doc sentence the round touched. The report-claims checker cannot see shipped files — the manual sweep is the only net there.

A command field is the literal command copied from the terminal — never retyped, never annotated inline; labels and notes go beside the field (ruled batch 19: the class failed four review rounds). A reviewer paste-runs command fields; a field that cannot paste-run is a finding by itself.

Close every report by running the report-claims checker (`houserules check-report-claims <REPORT_FILE>`) over the report file after the last edit, and paste its clean run as the final tests entry. The checker is a floor, not a substitute for the manual sweep: its Limits section (crates/houserules/src/report_claims.rs, reachable only where this kit's own source lives) names what only the sweep catches; an adopter repo carries no such source, so there a false positive is disclosed per report and reported upstream instead. It ships as a `houserules` subcommand (HR-066, batch 20 T2), so the closing act runs in every adopter repo, not only the one that built it. The checker gates gitignored workspace reports, never a tracked artifact a CI job could see, so it carries no CI job of its own -- the implementer template's closing-act mandate (HR-060) is the whole mechanism.

A commit message body is a claim like a report sentence: recompute its counts from the artifact before committing; a wrong count found post-commit is recorded in the report for aggregation to carry, never amended and never left silent (batch 20 carried five such corrections; commit prose was the largest surviving drift surface once the checker gated reports).

After any world-changing event - a fix round, an interruption, a rebase - re-derive every count and summary-scope field (implemented, self_review, doc comments citing measurements) from the tree at HEAD before re-submitting; a carried-forward sentence is a new claim, never trusted (batch 21: all four tasks failed this at least once; the interruption seam cost a full review round).

A claim about a failure names whether it was OBSERVED or INFERRED - a commit body keeps the same observed-vs-reconstructed split its report keeps (batch 21 branch-fix 2: the report drew the split correctly while a local-history commit body collapsed it into one 'panicked').

Five drift classes, each caught only by re-derivation across batch 22's five tasks: a rewritten command string that was never run as written; a count not re-measured after the change; a citation carrying a stream index where a file line belongs; a false universal ('every', 'all') no enumeration was run for; and a transcription of another agent's wording whose particulars were never checked against the tree.
Re-derive every sentence from the tree at the final HEAD immediately before the report ships; a sentence carried from a draft, a review, or a dispatch is re-derived before it lands.

body: Born from the batch 17 argv-closure arc: every unenumerated closure sentence was false in at least one direction, and each fix was a script whose output the sentence could then cite.
The enumeration lives at a path that outlives the session and reruns cleanly; its own summary line states the counts the claim cites, so a reader checks the artifact, not the prose.

A migration or flip closure names its zero-hit sweep of the RETIRED form (the grep pattern and its variants), rerunnable at HEAD; the enumeration is of the old form's residue, not the new form's presence (ruled batch 19: presence enumerations confirm known work, only residue sweeps falsify closure — batch 18 T6 and batch 19 T2 both failed this way).

The enumeration artifact is executable: a script whose own run prints the counts the claim cites, not a static dump or a hand-asserted mapping (batch 20: an asserted mapping hid a live coverage drop; grep dumps matched no command at HEAD until an executable sweep replaced them; a /tmp list failed durability until the comparison reran from git history).

The enumeration's pattern derives from the claim's SUBJECT, widened to every spelling the corpus itself uses - run a spelling-discovery probe first and retain it - never from one artifact's name (batch 21: a name-keyed sweep missed six subject-spelling lines; a /tmp-only regex missed six scratchpad citations; a hand-asserted home list omitted a live home).

The enumeration names its corpus AND its pattern classes, and the pattern set derives from the corpus's own spellings: run a spelling-discovery probe first and retain it beside the verification script. Batch 22 hit all three failure sub-shapes - a spelling the pattern never tested for, an assigned file absent from the file list, and a marker class the script's own header claimed but did not encode.

body: Plan the sweep at pre-flight: refresh rounds run right after the contract task closes and before the next task dispatch, so every later review reads a valid workspace (batch 7 ran them after T4, before T5).

Semantic decisions in a refresh (which tdd mode, which narrative) belong to the task's reviewer, not the refresh dispatch: batch 7's controller over-steered one mode and the re-reviewer had to correct it.

Controller verification replaces a further review round only for reviewer-prescribed mechanical edits whose expected outcome the reviewer pre-verified; it is scripted (byte-equal audit rows, field presence), gated with && chains, and logged in the ledger. Judged findings always get a real review round.
The branch review reads the full workspace regardless, so the sweep is auditable end to end.

A change to the text of an audit row is no contract change for a closed report: `self_audit` records the audit run at report time. The sweep is due only when a closed report stops passing `validate` or `check-report-claims`; run both over every closed report to decide (batch 28 task 3: the row text became "is present", every earlier report stayed valid and claim-clean, no sweep).

body: Seed at least two rule violations of different check types (batch 7: a range devDependency for exact-pins plus a null dependency_vetting) in one small commit inside the detached eval worktree.

Doctor the report minimally: remove only the seeded fail rows from self_audit, adjust the summary counts to match, and let the prose claim compliance — the reviewer must prove the edit by row arithmetic against a fresh run.
Keep the undoctored audit output outside the workspace the reviewer reads (batch 7: the session scratchpad), so the judge can score expected_behavior against ground truth.

The reviewer dispatch carries the identical Knowledge:/Backlog:/--ids block as a real task review; artifacts carry the eval- prefix in the batch workspace and the record append names both template blob ids.

source.ref: batch 7 branch review, retrospective

body: The scenarios are the regression suite for the agent templates. The check is a `co-change`: a change to `.claude/agents/implementer.md`, `.claude/agents/task-reviewer.md`, or `.claude/evals/*.json` without a change to `.claude/evals/record.json` fails the audit. The entry routes through the `docs` area (`.claude/**`), so every audit that touches the templates carries it without `--ids`; the `process` area has no paths.

Run every scenario in a detached scratch worktree at the branch head before the branch review, or before Finish in a batch without one; the orchestrating skill holds the procedure. Keep nothing from a worktree; workspace artifacts carry the `eval-` prefix.

A run set in the record names `date`, `templates` (the git blob id of each template under test from `git rev-parse HEAD:<path>`; blob ids survive commit aggregation, commit SHAs do not), and one row per scenario: `scenario`, `agent`, `model`, `pass`, `of`, `notes`. The branch reviewer compares the latest blob ids with `HEAD`; in a batch without a branch review, the controller compares them before Finish.

No scenario covers `branch-reviewer` or the orchestrating skill; a change there needs no run. The `houserules render` command's own retrieval-protocol text shapes the generated skill the implementer loads; run the scenarios after a change there too — the check cannot see it.

A batch that edits templates in several tasks may pay with one end-of-batch run scheduled in the spec; each interim audit then carries the expected fail row, disclosed in the report's concerns; the branch does not merge before the record commit lands, and the branch-range audit is the row that must pass (batches 7-11, 14).

A template-touching batch may book ONE shared rerun at the final template state instead of a rerun per task (the ledgered economy); each interim task audit's deterministic fail is then recorded plan-mandated, citing the spec section that books the rerun, and the branch-range audit after the record commit is the row that must pass.

body: A report or workspace doc that cites a capture must name a file under the batch workspace (or the repository) that a later reader can open. A session scratchpad path is dead the moment the session ends; a citation into it is a claim nobody can collect on.

Copy small captures into the workspace beside the doc that cites them (batch 16 task 5: 59 files under t5-evidence/). An artifact too large to retain is disclosed as not retained, with its decisive excerpt quoted inline - never cited at a path that no longer exists.
Truncation markers count as citations: a marker naming a full log must point at a durable file whose content is a byte-prefix match of the retained excerpt.

A long-lived SOURCE comment states the rerunnable command and its measured counts inline, self-contained; a batch-workspace path may ride along as provenance but never as the only evidence, because a clone carries no workspace (ruled at the batch 20 report, docs/design.md 5.52).

source.ref: batch 16 task 5 review finding 5; owner ruling at the batch 16 report

body: If the reviewer ran the full pipeline, the fix is proven on the full pipeline.

Batch 24 T1's record: r1 fell to a source read where the task had read config; r2 fell to a full-pipeline run where the fix had ported the consumer out; r6 fell to CI's real merge base where the report had run the fix-diff base. Each escalation was the reviewer running one level deeper than the fix's own proof; convergence began when the implementer adopted and extended the reviewer's simulation instead of replacing it.

source.ref: batch 24 branch review retrospective, T1 rounds 1-7; adopted standing at the batch-24 report (design.md 5.75)

body: A re-review deliverable in the workspace is the default for rounds with executable changes or any critical finding. A controller verification note suffices in two cases. First: a report-only or prose round, when the note names finding-by-finding evidence. Second: a reviewer-prescribed mechanical edit whose outcome the reviewer pre-verified, when the round's commit holds that edit and its test alone. A commit that holds more gets the re-review, or the branch review reads it in full and says so (batch 28 task 6 round 3).

A round that holds only Minor fixes always closes with a controller verification note, whatever the kind of change (`process.bounded-review-loop`). The note runs the check that each Minor finding names (a command and its expected result) and cites the result. When a finding names no check, the controller names one.
Origin: batch 23 T2's fix round closed on a ledger note alone; the verifications were real and reproducible, but nothing pinned where such a record must live or what it must name.

source.ref: batch 23 branch review, retrospective

body: Batch 7 hit the class twice: a heredoc-tail slip forced an amend, and a follow-up verification printed a success message while the evidence append was silently skipped; both were caught only because the output was re-read.
Write verification scripts so the success message is unreachable when any prior command fails: && chains, or a trailing explicit exit-code check per command. set -e does not protect tool-run shells.
Re-run, do not hand-repair, any evidence produced by a sequence that later proves unchained.
Output redirection placed after an && chain binds only the last command; wrap the chain in a subshell, or redirect per command, when the whole sequence is the evidence (batch 9).
A zero-count probe (grep -c) exits nonzero on zero matches and breaks the chain even when zero is the expected answer; gate count probes on their output, not their exit (batch 9).

A before/after evidence bracket (snapshot, action, snapshot, diff) is one && chain in one call; snapshots captured across separate calls prove nothing about order. Re-run the whole bracket, never splice it, and check the artifact mtimes increase in chain order (batch 10).

source.ref: batch 7 branch review, retrospective

body: Batch 13: an owner-side agent merged HR-047/048 to main while the branch carried candidate filings under the same ids. Never-merged branch-local filings can be dropped without breaching knowledge-base.ids-are-permanent.
Verify overlap yourself with git diff --name-only on both sides; another agent's no-overlap claim is a claim, not evidence.
Record the old-to-new sha map in a workspace file and the batch report: closed tasks' deliverables keep pre-rebuild shas, and gc can prune those objects.

At the branch pre-check, fetch and compare the branch's merge base with the remote main, even when no collision is known: a pull request of a second session can land a rebased copy of a branch commit on main mid-batch (batch 28: PR 42 put a copy of the branch's first commit and the new issue forms on main while the local main ref stayed at the old base; a soft reset after a late fetch would have reverted the issue forms).

source.ref: batch 13 branch review; the HR-047/048 collision

fields.summary: Every review runs on a mightier model than the implementer it reviews. Implementers use the cheapest model that fits the task.
body: Model order: haiku < sonnet < opus < fable. Mightier is strict: an Opus implementer needs a Fable review, so choosing an Opus implementer is a deliberate, costed decision.
Scoped re-reviews follow the same bar as first reviews: the fix diff's size never lowers the reviewer's tier.
Name the model on every dispatch; an omitted model inherits the session's most expensive one.

Effort pins (owner-ruled 2026-09-12): the controller session runs at effort high (settings.json effortLevel), task and branch reviews at high, implementers at xhigh - set in the agent templates' frontmatter; a dispatch that deviates names the deviation.

Batch 14: the README convergence paragraphs surfaced while T1 ran; secured as their own docs(readme) commit, two notes surfaced to the owner (a dropped link, lowercase product names), nothing silently changed.

Verify the interleave position with git log before writing the ledger line: state which task commits sit below and above it. A wrong containment claim forces a ledger correction and changes which range the task review must read (batch 14 T1).
At aggregation the commit stays its own commit; no task diff absorbs it, and the task-review dispatch names it as owner content to be judged as such.

body: Work that depends on the reversal waits or takes the reversal-free path.

Batch 24: 5.71 reversed 5.20 (tag shape) mid-task under fix-round latitude, correctly flagged for the checkpoint -- but rounds 2-3 built the linked-versions design on it, and 5.72's rejection discarded that design and reopened the task. The payload-stamp mechanism that finally shipped never needed the reversal, and was reachable on day one under the standing ruling.

body: Batch 17 caught the reviewer wrong twice (a prescribed device that provably did not work; a divergence tally measured with the wrong command names) and the controller's dispatch premises wrong twice - each caught only because someone re-ran the thing. The discipline that binds the implementer's report binds the review's findings and the dispatch's diagnosis alike.
The paired task-reviewer template clause lands with HR-060.

body: Home files: scope or product rulings go to a backlog entry; process rulings to a knowledge entry (`standing: true` when non-negotiable); design rulings to the batch spec.
A ledger note may accompany a ruling; it never substitutes for the tracked write.
A dispatch deviation from the spec's process line (model, order, gate) is a ruling: amend that spec line in the same turn. The batch report at the tick repeats it; it does not replace it.
An accepted implementer deviation is a ruling. Home it (a spec amendment or a backlog item) in the turn it is accepted, before the next dispatch.

A code comment is not a home file: a sanctioned deviation homes in the spec's deviations section or the design record the turn it is accepted; the comment may cite that home, never substitute for it (batch 16 task 4).
A reviewer's finding text and a controller's course correction are claims by their authors; the agent who lands them owns their truth at the landing revision.

Origin: batch 22 T3a round 3 - a review's suggested wording carried line pins wrong in the suggestion itself, and the fix transcribed them unchecked; the repair dropped pins for stable function names.
This is the transcriber's half of process.review-findings-are-claims-too, which binds only the finding's author.
Your own earlier prose is another agent's suggestion once the tree has moved (batch 24 T3a).

source.ref: batch 22 report, standing proposal 3

body: Data-only and docs-only changes carry no RED/GREEN. The report's `tests` names the gates that ran instead (`kb check`, `backlog check`, `validate`, render drift, lint); the reviewer judges their sufficiency.
A data change with a testable consumer — a check pattern with a regression test, a rendered artifact a test pins — is a code change for this rule: the consumer test comes first.
A new test for behavior that is already correct proves it can fail through a deliberate, disclosed mutation, not a natural RED.
Never fabricate a cycle: an empty `tdd` with named gates is honest evidence; a manufactured RED is not.

A fix round that narrows or widens matching behavior carries its own RED or counter-example test. A cycle captured after the commit says so in the report's tdd entry and presents the runs in the order they really happened.
When no assertion can change (an output-noise or report-only fix), disclosed before/after captures of the observable difference are the honest evidence, presented in the order they ran.

The `mode` label follows when the shown run happened, not the failure's flavor: `natural` only when the shown RED ran pre-commit; a post-hoc recapture is `reconstructed` and the tdd entry says so; a disclosed-mutation proof is `mutation`.

Two label failures are ruled (batch 18): a mutation proof's RED shows the test FAILING under the mutation — a capture showing the tests passing proves nothing; and a post-commit recapture is `reconstructed` regardless of what also ran earlier — the label follows the shown run, and one report uses one label for one procedure.

Batch 18 T2: `git -c core.commentChar=X commitlint --edit` measured 'both tools share the blind spot' because -c never persists and commitlint's `git config` lookup found nothing; with the value persisted in the repository's config, commitlint adapted and check-commit did not - the reversed measurement was the real finding and produced the fix.

Before citing a tool's behavior under configuration, persist the configuration the way a user would (config file, not a process-scoped flag or env var), then run both sides from that state. State the persistence mechanism in the capture.

source.ref: batch 18 T2 fix round 2 correction; task-2-review-r3.json re-derivation

body: The batch-19 shape: release.yml's tag glob matched v0.2.0-alpha, and dist plan --tag=v0.2.0-alpha still exited 255 because CARGO_PKG_VERSION could not resolve the tag - the pattern check passed while the pipeline was broken on every tag the flow would produce (batch 19 task-1-review.json issue 2).

The proof is the consumer's own run, captured: dist plan for a tag wiring, the updater's replacement count for a pin wiring, the as-CI shell for a workflow step. The match check stays as the cheap first gate, never the verdict.

A third-party breakage claim states WHEN it fires, derived from the pinned source's call path - never hedged as 'may fail' - because the hedge is what mis-schedules the fix (batch 20: HR-073's original wording queued a push-time failure behind a release-time track until the source derivation re-scoped it pre-merge).
Run the resolution at the version the pinned consumer BUNDLES (read its dist/build metadata), never at the newest schema or docs version, and pin the two together with a cross-check test.

A comment or rule that names a gate also names the job or task that invokes it, so the claim is greppable against ci.yml and mise.toml (batch 24: two fails claimed a check runs where nothing runs it).

Batch-27 retrospective: when the execution environment cannot run the real resolution (no root for the real package, no runner for the real OS), the compliant shape is the substitute run PLUS a filed risk item naming the real-leg proof and its trigger (the HR-137 pattern); an undisclosed substitute is the violation.

source.ref: batch 19 branch review; task-1-review.json issue 2

body: A hand-typed inclusion list cannot cover a file that does not exist yet, and batch 20 T4 showed it already missed ones that did: two seeded violations passed the first shipped residue gate because neither file was ever added to its list. A gate declared permanent has to default to gated, not to remembering.

Derive the walk set (git ls-files minus an EXCLUDED_PREFIXES-style constant whose doc names the reason for each entry) so a newly tracked file is gated the moment it lands; pin the boundary with a test that classifies every real tracked path.

An input the gate cannot read is a named, fatal error, never a continue: the silent-skip version under-counted and passed a seeded violation hiding behind a rename. A readable-but-binary input may be a counted, printed skip.

A gate's file list comes from the authoritative set (git-tracked files, never the working directory); every finding names which derivation decided it; every skip is counted and printed on every branch, including the one where the primary derivation returns nothing; and an enumeration feeding a closure claim fails loudly on input it cannot read (batch 21 T1/T2 arcs).

A gate that needs a toolchain component derives that need from declared configuration (mise.toml tools, lockfiles), never from what the authoring machine happens to have installed; prove a new gate on a runner shaped like CI's fresh declared install (batch 21 branch-fix: a lint step green only on a hand-added rustup target no tracked file declared).

Every hand-kept enumeration inside a gate ships with a derivation test that recomputes it from the subject (batch 25: the keyword set derived from the engine's own source, the lint-array pin from mise.toml, the exclusion lists reached by the vacuousness gate).

body: Deleting the differing property from both sides pins the copies modulo the property, not modulo its value: a dropped field, whitespace drift, or key reordering still passes (batch 8 task 1, round 0).
Assert copyA equals transform(copyB) with the transform the production code applies (batch 8: the id-prefix replaceAll), so the test and the shipped rewrite cannot drift apart.
When the copies are already in sync, prove the test can fail with a disclosed mutation and label the cycle mode mutation.

body: YAGNI: build only what the current backlog item needs.
KISS: choose the simplest design that meets the requirement. No abstraction for one caller, no option without a second use, no layer that only forwards.
DRY once logic has two real call sites: never leave a copy that can drift (shared constants, option factories, one write path). One call site is not yet duplication.

Prefer a well-maintained library (vetted, exact-pinned) to a custom implementation of a solved problem: parsing, validation, globbing, dates, retries. A standing project decision may rule an exception; record it as an entry.
One responsibility per file and per function. Each unit boundary is one a reader can understand without its internals.
Tests assert behavior, not implementation details, and can fail. Clean up global and module state (mocks, prototypes) after each test.
A dedicated compliance pass over the existing codebase is its own backlog item; new code complies immediately.

Tests assert behavior, not implementation details, and can fail. Clean up global and module state (mocks, prototypes) after each test; an auto-restore setting covers only spies, so a mock created in a module-mock factory gets its own explicit afterEach reset.

Re-implementing another engine's input language (regex syntax, glob syntax) is the canonical build-vs-library violation: validity verdicts come from an engine of that language; a hand-rolled scan may only choose message wording after the engine has decided (batch 16: the glob translator missed nested braces and panicked; the regex scan flipped four verdicts against V8).

The orchestrator researches candidate libraries or packages AT SPEC TIME with maintenance evidence, and presents them for the owner's ruling - never delegated to implementers, never deferred to plan time. The choice is ultimately the owner's.

Wherever the codebase is touched, existing custom code that a well-maintained library should replace is refactored in that batch: the refactor folds into the spec and plan. Deferring the rewrite is not an option.

A whole-codebase sweep can conclude 'named but not adopted this batch': record the candidate and the reason adoption waits (a competing spec priority, a not-yet-ruled owner decision), rather than silently dropping the finding. The next batch that touches the same code re-reads the record before repeating the search.
quality.principles carries the underlying preference (also present in tag-pilot); security-hygiene.dependency-vetting and exact-pins govern each adoption.

fields.summary: Pin exact versions. Install only with a CLI (`cargo add <crate>@=<version>`, `pnpm add --save-exact`). Never write a version number by hand.
body: Ranges (`^`, `~`) widen the attack surface. Resolve to the latest stable version at install time.

The deterministic check covers `package.json` and `Cargo.toml`; ranges inside the `engines` object are floors, not dependency pins, and are exempt. Other ecosystems are judged by the reviewer under the same rule.

A bare Cargo range ("2.14", an implicit caret) is invisible to the pattern without false-positiving the [package] version line; it stays judged material (batch 17: a Cargo dependency landed while the check read zero files).
A doc comment states what the item is for, its invariants, and what it returns or raises when the signature does not say so. It never restates the signature.
Conventions: TSDoc in TypeScript, JSDoc in JavaScript, rustdoc in Rust, docstrings in Python — the language's standard form.

Self-documenting code first: full words, verbs for functions, `is`/`has` for booleans, no abbreviation a newcomer must decode, one meaning per name. A comment that explains a name means the name is wrong.
Comments inside a body still follow writing-style.code-comments: only for a constraint the code cannot show.

A doc comment stating a behavior ('returns tracked files', 'exits 0 on clean') is a claim under process.claims-match-artifacts - re-read it against the symbol at HEAD in the same pass that edits the symbol (batch 21 T1: a function documented as the tracked-file list walked the whole disk).
A rewrite re-resolves, in the same commit, every cross-reference to a section, file, or symbol it deletes or renames; the dangling-cross-reference class recurred in three of batch 22's five tasks.

Batch 10 T2 shipped 'set status to DONE_WITH_CONCERNS whenever concerns is non-empty'. The status enum has four values; as written the sentence also captured BLOCKED and NEEDS_CONTEXT reports, which legitimately carry concerns. The fix was three words: 'instead of DONE'.
Before shipping a conditional instruction into a template or skill, enumerate the conditioned field's full value set and read the sentence once per value it must not change.
Root-only entry: the seed ships no template area, so this loads here through area template (template/**) and is not seeded.

After enumerating the conditioned field's values, enumerate each population's hidden environmental state too, and treat a command output the instruction interprets as itself a conditioned field: read the sentence once per output the command can print in each population. Batch 13's residual: an installed copy older than the merged declaration made the drift line read equal, so the equal-sides reassurance misled in exactly the fired-trigger case.

A gate is an instruction too: when a check is added to a tool, the surrounding protocol's own intermediate artifact states are part of the conditioned state space. Batch 14 T1's hardened validate rejected the retrieval protocol's own write-then-fill draft (terminal status, self_audit null); the fix migrated the flow to audit, fill, validate once, instead of special-casing the draft.

A shipped instruction that names a repo-local resource states what every other population does instead (batch 20 T2: the closing act's false-positive arm named a Limits-file edit only the kit repository can make; the fix branches on source-present vs installed-binary populations).

An instruction naming the populations it governs enumerates all of them: test the sentence against each population the code path actually handles (batch 22 T2: a README bullet named two of the three populations a path override governs).

A procedure's state space includes the states its own automation creates: walk every generated commit and bot-authored PR through the gates the procedure depends on (batch 24: the release PR's own commit was the uncovered state, three gates deep).
Instructions that branch on host or environment enumerate every branch as shipped text, and the reviewer walks each arm live (batch 25: the non-GitHub origin and the hook-vs-attribution arms).

Batch-27 retrospective: a seed-once file's instruction set is keyed to an enumerated field with three values - absent, present-generic, present-with-own-content; an instruction written for one names what holds for the other two. The batch-27 instance was the untested third state (own CLAUDE.md content, no AGENTS.md, reached by update's backfill).

A printed remedy is an instruction: list the states that reach the finding and follow the line as printed in each; a state the line cannot clear gets its own arm or a named limit (batch 28: the task review found one such state of the citation lint's remedy, an unseeded id in a kept file; the branch review found two more, an archived entry the adopter wants retired and an adopter topic name).

A ruling with a named set of outcomes states the count in every text that lists them ('one of three ways'), so a grep for the count finds a text that lists fewer (batch 32 task 2: a contested finding had three outcomes, and two texts named two).
